speaker_role: former Stanford alumni interviewer (one admissions cycle), now running a college consulting business (Athena Admits)
commercial_incentive: Speaker co-ran a college consulting business while at Stanford; channel (Athena Admits) appears to be a college admissions consultancy
key_insights: Interviewers are coached to start scoring near the middle of the scale; giving a 1 (terrible) or 5 (extraordinary) rating is rare, so an interview usually can't sink an otherwise strong application but can add positive color

For Stanford specifically, the interviewer is given almost no information beforehand beyond the applicant's name and high school; other schools like Harvard give interviewers a questionnaire tied to the application
Recommends casual/comfortable public locations (e.g., coffee shop) over formal settings, since Stanford explicitly advises against overly formal venues
Advises preparing exactly three specific personal stories you want to ensure come up, since interviewers are trying to remember what makes you distinct among many similar high-stat applicants
Recommends using the STAR framework (situation, task, action, result) to structure anecdotes so they are memorable to a possibly tired or distracted interviewer
Suggests researching each school's distinct culture/personality beforehand (e.g., Stanford described as quirky and less grade-focused, MIT as academically rigid, Yale as artsy) to tailor answers
Interviewers are volunteers and often nervous themselves, evaluating primarily whether they can picture the applicant fitting into campus life rather than focusing on GPA/test scores
Recommends heavy mock-interview practice and sending a specific, personalized thank-you note afterward
notable_or_distinctive: Gives an insider description of how alumni interviewers are actually coached to score (rarely using score extremes) and the practice of researching a school's specific 'personality' to tailor interview answers.
reliability_notes: Based on a single interviewer's one year of experience at one school, generalized to interviews broadly; speaker likely has a commercial interest in college consulting via Athena Admits; minor auto-caption errors (e.g., 'recent software update' likely meant 'recent self').
